citations.quote: OPAL is a MBSE software tool based on the SAPPhIRE Model for the capture, management, representation and sharing of conceptual design data.
The results of the study show that the students were able to effectively utilize OPAL's functions with only a short introduction, with 85% reporting it easy to use.

In contrast to their traditional file management software and practices, the visual representation of the data via the SAPPhIRE Models made it significantly easier to be able to track and find data using the causal links, regardless of the subsystem being studied.
Initial testing based on the UPEI SpudNik-1 CubeSat project shows promise for OPAL's use in supporting concurrent conceptual design.

The model was designed to provide a rich representation of a system at different levels of abstraction. Of particular interest is its use of three fundamental aspects for illustrating causality, function, structure and behaviour, with the latter serving as the common link between the other two, viewing "behavior as the link between function and structure defined at a given level." [15].
Previous work has confirmed that the SAPPhIRE model was capable, at least from high level of abstraction, to provide a basic representation of the behaviour of CubeSat subsystems [16].

All work for this survey took place at the University of Prince Edward Island (UPEI) using the CubeSat 'SpudNik-1'as a case study. The first major design review, the Mission Concept Review, was taken as a reference point marking the end of the conceptual design phase.

The survey commenced with the capturing of all digital CubeSat data, via a shared drive. Once the data was cloned onto a local hard-drive, every file was systematically investigated and evaluated on whether it fit the description of the SAPPhIRE model elements. All other data, such as monetary budgets and schedules, was ignored for this study. The relevant information was then collected and rearranged based on its relation to model elements, an example of which is shown in Table 1.

citations.quote: Another limiting factor of the survey was, while thorough, it could not capture file versions or represent the evolution of the design files. The SAPPhIRE models created are the end state of the conceptual design phase.
Clearly a collaborative tool must be able to easily access and represent this data to be effective as a design support software.

A software tool was therefore created to support and facilitate conceptual design activities and collaboration, based on the behavioural models of the CubeSat subsystems and the results of the data survey.

citations.quote: As seen in [17], SAPPhIRE models are linked via their Inputs and States. A change of state can transform the input of a connected subsystem, and vice versa. This is a crucial feature for illustrating causal relationships between subsystems. The initial effort was thus directed towards creating these inter-subsystem connections.
CEDESK [18] was used as a reference for the creation of OPAL's subsystem views, including both the Java libraries and how data was defined and linked between subsystems.

Each element block in each system model is connected to the relevant conceptual design data, as summarized in Table 2. For example, in Fig. 4, the user has selected the "Power Inputs" in the input block, which retrieved the relevant section of the CubeSat Power Budget spreadsheet, shown as text in the bottom part of the screen.

While these connections were made manually for the proof-of-concept tool, future iterations will allow for user created links and a simplified update process to manage iterations. At the moment, these connections are made with the live files, so iterations are not tracked within OPAL.

citations.quote: The objective of the trials was to evaluate the effectiveness of OPAL as a conceptual design support tool, and to propose recommendations for its improvement. The expectation was that the student participants would find OPAL to be a preferable alternative for managing data, especially when operating outside of the subsystem for which they were responsible.

The participants involved in the study were recruited from the UPEI student engineering body. Ethics approval was obtained from the UPEI Research Ethics Board. Participants ranged from third year engineering students to graduate level researchers and tested independently. Based upon a power analysis, and similar studies from literature [19], the total number of participants was set at 15.

The testing procedure involved a $ \sim 1 5 $ -min introduction to the SAPPhIRE model and OPAL, and then immediately proceeded to the evaluation, which took an average of 45 min. Students were then asked to complete the survey on their own time to maximum feedback quality.
The first segment required participants to navigate OPAL's user interface and locate a file.
The second segment explored the elements and interfaces of OPAL. Participants are asked to trace the data flow, using interfaces both within and between the subsystem models.
The last segment made participants explain the potential change propagation stemming from a defined change to the system.
Every question evaluated the effectiveness of OPAL in a certain category, with '7' signifying a strong agreeance with its effectiveness in said category, and '1' indicating strong disagreement.

citations.quote: The high scores seen for each question is especially encouraging when considering that each participant only had an average of 15 min to become familiar with SAPPhIRE and OPAL. Additionally, although 5/15 participants had no previous experience working on the CubeSat, their quantitative results were not found to differentiate significantly upon the evaluation of the product moment correlation coefficient for both CubeSat familiarity and education level factors.
The standardized, visual layout of OPAL made it easier to navigate and locate data, even when operating outside of the subsystem of expertise.
For instance, to source the power allocated to the image sensor, participants used both the EPS output and the Payload Subsystem's input elements.

Consequently, many struggled during this segment as can be seen in the relatively low quantitative scores. However, the second task of the segment was generally well understood by the users, after the explanation of the desired solution for the first part was explained.

The visualization of all the subsystems made it easier to understand the relationship and its interactions between each subsystem. Therefore tracking how a change to one component could affect the subsystem and components was easy.
OPAL has very limited representation of the extensive requirements found in the CubeSat project. It cannot be used as an effective requirements verification tool in this state.

This paper presented the reasoning, development, and evaluation of the novel software tool OPAL, which allows designers to connect conceptual causal models directly to the relevant design data, using their understanding of the system behaviour, rather than the product structure, to organize and navigate product information.

The quantitative results show strong comprehension and effective use of OPAL's SAPPhIRE based framework as a data support structure. The results indicate that OPAL can integrate the data files to create a sufficiently detailed system model.

Considering that the students had an average of fifteen minutes to learn the intricacies of SAPPhIRE, the results are encouraging for further research. This indicates how future SAPPhIRE based tools may not require substantial resources to train users.
Future work could explore how SAPPhIRE can represent digital information flow in later stages of the lifecycle, as well as integrating a SQL server to allow for concurrent use and collaboration.
At the very least, the concept of a simplified representation of an entire system has been shown to be feasible using SAPPhIRE.

The SAPPhIRE model element titles were found to be a source of confusion for users. The Organ in particular could be renamed to better reflect its purpose, such as 'Physical Parameters'. The 'Physical Phenomena' also created initial confusion, and could be renamed 'Subsystem Behaviour', or something similar. A more efficient method of introducing and explaining the SAPPhIRE model and the concept of causal models would significantly aid in the effectiveness of both OPAL and any future software.

As a result, a parallel tool built upon alternate ontology and semantics would be needed for requirements management, possibly creating an integration issue between OPAL and other data tools. A possible solution may be to introduce new ontology to OPAL to give it the ability to represent these features.

This is one of the limitations with conducting a survey using engineering students. In an industry setting, where the database may need to be accessed and understood by external personnel, the Physical Phenomena may prove to be more relevant.

The task was more complex; the approach to solving it was not well defined, and the concept of causality was generally not familiar to the participants. Additionally, the subjects had limited experience with this concept being applied via a MBSE or PLM tool.
